questions.subject: Ethics
questions.chapter: Code of Ethics - Responding to Non-Compliance with Laws and Regulations (NOCLAR) by professional accountants in business
questions.topic: Duty of a CFO (senior CA in employment) who knows of an environmental breach
questions.ask: CA G, the CFO, knew floatable solids were 4 mm against a 3 mm norm, gave one instruction, did no follow-up and did not tell management. A government notice followed. What was his responsibility?

options.a: Not liable - it is the production head's job, and CA G is not in practice
options.b: As a CA, the CFO had to investigate the matter, inform those charged with governance of the results and keep documentation
options.c: CA G had to inform those charged with governance and keep documentation
options.d: Not liable as he is not in practice and has no duty on such non-compliance; only a moral duty as employee to inform TCWG

questions.clue: CFO was aware of this fact but failed to disclose the same to the management
think: Breach of environmental law noticed by a CA in a job = NOCLAR for a senior professional accountant in business (Part 2 of the Code).
Chapter clear -> Audit SM, Professional Ethics -> NOCLAR -> 'senior professional accountants in business'.
Code: obtain an understanding of the matter, discuss with superior, get it communicated to TCWG and rectified, document it - 'not in practice' is no excuse.
(B) has all three steps - understand/investigate, inform TCWG, document; (A) and (D) are excuses the Code rejects.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit - Professional Ethics (Code of Ethics, NOCLAR for professional accountants in business)

questions.solve: The NOCLAR section for CAs in business covers CA G as CFO (a senior professional accountant). On becoming aware of suspected non-compliance (floatable solids 4 mm vs 3 mm norm, risk of heavy environmental penalties) he must: (1) obtain an understanding of the matter - what happened, which law, likely consequences; (2) discuss with his superior; (3) take steps to have it communicated to those charged with governance, rectified and prevented from recurring; (4) document the matter, discussions and responses. CA G only gave an instruction, did not follow up after three months and kept management in the dark - he failed this duty. Being an employee and not in practice does not exempt him.
questions.answer: (B) As a CA, the CFO had to investigate the matter, inform those charged with governance about the results and keep documentation. [ICAI also accepted (C).]
questions.flag: ICAI accepted two keys; (B) is the fuller statement of the Code (understand + communicate + document), (C) drops the 'understand/investigate' step.
questions.trap: Choosing (A) or (D) because CA G is 'not in practice' - the NOCLAR section for CAs in business applies to him.

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Companies Act, 2013 - Sections 188/189 (contracts with interested directors, register in Form MBP-4) with CARO 2020
questions.topic: Licence fee to a director for his logo - register entry and CARO reporting
questions.ask: DSL pays its director Mr. B Rs 25 lakh a year to use his logo but did not enter the contract in the register of contracts in which directors are interested. Is entry needed, and is it reportable under CARO?

options.a: Neither entry in the register nor CARO reporting is required
options.b: Entry in the register is required and it is reportable under CARO
options.c: Entry in the register is required but it is not reportable under CARO
options.d: Entry in the register is not required but it is reportable under CARO

questions.clue: register maintained for recording contracts or arrangements in which directors are interested
think: Contract with a director = related party (s.2(76)); the register for such contracts is s.189 (Form MBP-4).
Chapter clear -> SPOM-A Companies Act -> 'section 189', then Audit SM -> CARO 2020 clause 3(xiii).
Rs 25 lakh licence of the director's logo is a s.188 contract; the s.189(5) exemption is only for goods/services up to Rs 5 lakh a year -> entry needed.
Statutory auditor has already 'noted it for CARO' -> related party reporting under clause 3(xiii) -> (B); ICAI also accepted (A).

look_up.where: SPOM-A Corporate Laws - Companies Act ss.184, 188, 189; ICAI SM Audit - CARO 2020

questions.solve: Mr. B is a director, so he is a related party u/s 2(76). Paying him Rs 25 lakh a year for a licence to use his logo is a contract to which s.188 applies (use of his property/availing his services). S.189(1) requires particulars of every such contract to be entered in the register (Form MBP-4); the s.189(5) carve-out is only for goods/services up to Rs 5 lakh a year, so it does not apply. Hence entry was required. Under CARO 2020 clause 3(xiii) the auditor reports whether all related party transactions comply with ss.177/188 and are disclosed in the financial statements; the statutory auditor has noted the lapse for this.
questions.answer: (B) The payment must be entered in the register u/s 189 and is reportable by the statutory auditor under CARO (clause 3(xiii)). [ICAI also accepted (A).]
questions.flag: Split key: CARO 2020 has no clause on the s.189 register itself (CARO 2003 had one), so reporting rests on clause 3(xiii); (A) is hard to defend under s.189.
questions.trap: Ticking (C) - the register point is right, but CARO 3(xiii) on related party transactions makes it reportable.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: Foreign Trade Policy - Duty Exemption Schemes (Advance Authorisation)
questions.topic: AA eligibility (no export-history condition, no value cap) and discharge of export obligation
questions.ask: DSL wants to import upgraded chips (FOB Rs 95 lakh) duty-free under Advance Authorisation and meet the export obligation by supplying laptops with the existing chip to Noida SEZ. Can it?

options.a: No - AA cannot be issued as DSL has not exported for a continuous period of three years
options.b: Yes, AA up to Rs 90 lakh only; supply to Noida SEZ cannot count towards export obligation
options.c: Yes, AA for the entire Rs 95 lakh; supply to Noida SEZ counts towards export obligation
options.d: Yes, AA for the entire Rs 95 lakh; but supply to Noida SEZ cannot count towards export obligation

questions.clue: supply the laptops (with existing technology chip) to Noida Technology SEZ
think: 'Advance authorization' + 'export obligation' -> FTP Chapter 4, duty exemption schemes (IDT).
Chapter clear -> IDT SM -> Foreign Trade Policy -> Advance Authorisation -> eligibility and export obligation.
AA has no 3-year export record condition and no value cap -> (A), (B) out; AA for the full Rs 95 lakh is fine.
AA inputs must be physically incorporated in the export product; laptops with the OLD chip do not use the imported chip -> cannot discharge EO -> (D).

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT - Foreign Trade Policy (Advance Authorisation)

questions.solve: AA allows duty-free import of inputs that are physically incorporated in the export product (allowing normal wastage). It is issued to a manufacturer exporter or a merchant exporter tied to a supporting manufacturer. There is no condition of past exports for three years and no fixed value limit, so DSL can get AA for the full Rs 95 lakh (its small exports of Rs 25-35 lakh do not matter). But the export obligation must be met with products that use the imported inputs. DSL plans to supply laptops fitted with the existing chip, not the imported upgraded chip, so these supplies cannot discharge the obligation under this authorisation.
questions.answer: (D) Yes, AA can be issued for the entire Rs 95 lakh, but the supply of these laptops to Noida Technology SEZ cannot be counted towards the export obligation.
questions.flag: Know the real reason: supply to an SEZ generally counts as physical export for AA under the FTP; it fails here because the laptops do not carry the imported chip.
questions.trap: Thinking AA needs an export track record (A) or is capped at a lower value like Rs 90 lakh (B).

questions.subject: FR
questions.chapter: Ind AS 34 Interim Financial Reporting read with Ind AS 10 Events after the Reporting Period
questions.topic: Government clarification on GST rate after period-end - adjusting event in condensed interim statements
questions.ask: DSL charged 12% GST on wallets sold up to 30.09.2024; before the interim statements were approved, the government clarified 18%. Management refuses to adjust or disclose. Is that right?

options.a: Yes - condensed interim statements need not be adjusted for events after the reporting date
options.b: Yes - no adjustment needed; disclosure in notes is enough
options.c: No - these are adjusting events; adjust the interim statements even though condensed
options.d: No - adjust or disclose depending on gravity and amount; a full set would have been adjusted

questions.clue: government issued a clarification to tax such wallets @ GST 18%
think: Event after 30.09.2024 but before approval -> Ind AS 10; 'condensed interim' -> Ind AS 34.
Chapter clear -> FR SM -> Ind AS 10 adjusting vs non-adjusting; Ind AS 34 'same accounting policies as annual'.
The clarification creates no new liability - it confirms the 18% that already applied to sales made before 30.09.2024 -> condition existed at reporting date -> adjusting.
Ind AS 34 uses the same recognition and measurement as annual statements; condensed means fewer notes, not less recognition -> (C).

look_up.where: ICAI SM FR - Ind AS 10 and Ind AS 34

questions.solve: Ind AS 10: events between the end of the period and the approval date that give evidence of conditions existing at the end of the period are adjusting events. GST at 18% was payable on the wallets already sold by 30.09.2024; the department's notice and the clarification only confirm that liability. So DSL must provide for the short-paid 6% GST (and interest, if any) in the interim statements. Ind AS 34 requires the same recognition and measurement principles as in annual statements; being condensed only reduces disclosures. Management's stand is wrong.
questions.answer: (C) No - these are adjusting events; the interim financial statements must be adjusted even though they are condensed.
questions.trap: Treating it as a change in tax rate after the period (non-adjusting) - it clarifies the rate that already applied on the sales.

questions.subject: DT
questions.chapter: Tax audit u/s 44AB - Form 3CD (with ss.269SS, 40A(3A), 41(1), 56(2)(ix))
questions.topic: Which items need reporting in Form 3CD
questions.ask: Which issues need reporting in Form 3CD: (a) ICD Rs 80 lakh by a/c payee cheque; (b) warranty provision Rs 18 lakh with suit pending; (c) Rs 60,000 accrued last year, paid in cash this year in one day; (d) Rs 20 lakh advance for sale of investment plot, now time-barred?
questions.clue: Tax Audit team also raised some issues for the year ending 31st March 2025
think: 'Tax audit' -> Form 3CD; test each item against a 3CD clause.
Chapter clear -> DT SM index: 'section 269SS', '40A(3A)', '56(2)(ix)', '41(1)'; map to 3CD clauses 31, 21(g), 21(d).

(a) every loan/deposit above Rs 20,000 is reported with its mode, even by a/c payee cheque; (b) warranty with suit pending = contingent liability; (c) cash paid next year above limit = deemed income u/s 40A(3A).
(d) advance not forfeited, only time-barred, and not a trading liability -> neither s.56(2)(ix) nor s.41(1) -> not reportable -> (D).

look_up.where: ICAI SM DT - PGBP (s.40A(3A), s.41(1)), Other Sources (s.56(2)(ix)), s.269SS; Form 3CD

questions.solve: (a) ICD Rs 80 lakh: clause 31(a) asks for each loan/deposit accepted above the s.269SS limit with its mode - reportable even though received by account payee cheque. (b) Warranty provision Rs 18 lakh under litigation is a liability of a contingent nature - clause 21(g) - reportable. (c) Rs 60,000 allowed in FY 2023-24 on accrual and paid in cash in one day in FY 2024-25 - above the Rs 10,000 (Rs 35,000 for transporters) limit, so deemed income u/s 40A(3A) - clause 21(d) - reportable. (d) Rs 20 lakh advance for sale of a capital asset is not forfeited (s.56(2)(ix)) and is not a trading liability (s.41(1)) - nothing to report.
questions.answer: (D) Issues (a), (b) and (c).
questions.trap: Treating the time-barred advance as income - s.56(2)(ix) needs forfeiture, and s.41(1) covers only trading liabilities.

questions.subject: Audit
questions.chapter: SA 510 Initial Audit Engagements - Opening Balances (with SA 705)
questions.topic: Opening inventory in a first-year audit; modified opinions
questions.ask: New auditor CA Shankar found weak controls over inventory as on 1.4.2024. State extra procedures for opening inventory, and his course of action if (a) no evidence is obtained, (b) opening inventory is materially misstated, (c) the company calls it a change in accounting policy.
questions.clue: Till last financial year, DEF & Associates were carrying out both the audits
think: New auditor + opening balance = initial audit engagement -> SA 510.
Chapter clear -> Audit SM -> SA 510 -> 'opening inventory'; then SA 705 for which modified opinion.
Write four blocks matching the four asks: procedures / no evidence / misstatement / change in policy.
Use case words: DEF & Associates (predecessor), count on 30-31 March 2025, inventory as on 1.4.2024.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit - SA 510 Initial Audit Engagements - Opening Balances

questions.solve: SA 510 objective: get sufficient appropriate evidence that opening balances do not contain misstatements that materially affect the current year. Work on closing stock gives little evidence about opening stock, so extra procedures are needed: review DEF & Associates' working papers (if they share them); observe the current count (attended on 30-31 March 2025) and roll back to 1.4.2024 quantities using receipts and issues in between; test valuation of opening items (cost records, NRV, consistency of method); gross profit analysis and cut-off checks around 1.4.2024. Outcomes under SA 705: (1) evidence cannot be obtained -> qualified opinion or disclaimer; (2) material misstatement in opening stock not properly accounted, presented or disclosed -> qualified or adverse; (3) change in accounting policy: if not consistently applied to opening balances or not properly accounted, presented or disclosed (Ind AS 8) -> qualified or adverse; if the change is justified, applied consistently and disclosed -> no modification.
questions.answer:
1. SA 510: in an initial audit, CA Shankar must get sufficient appropriate evidence that opening balances (inventory on 1.4.2024) have no material misstatement affecting 2024-25.
2. Additional procedures for opening inventory:
(a) Review working papers of predecessor DEF & Associates for the 31.3.2024 count and valuation.
(b) Use the count observed on 30-31 March 2025 and reconcile back to opening quantities (roll-back using purchases, production and sales).
(c) Test valuation of opening inventory items (cost records, NRV, same method as this year).
(d) Gross profit ratio analysis and cut-off tests around 1.4.2024.
3. If evidence is not obtained: qualified opinion or disclaimer of opinion, as appropriate (SA 705).
4. If opening inventory is materially misstated and the effect is not properly accounted for, presented or disclosed: qualified or adverse opinion (SA 705).
5. If claimed as a change in accounting policy: check the change is allowed by Ind AS 8, applied consistently to opening balances and properly accounted and disclosed. If yes - no modification. If not - qualified or adverse opinion.
Conclusion: try roll-back and valuation procedures first; modify the opinion only as per SA 705.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI; reviewing the predecessor's working papers is an extra valid SA 510 procedure added here.
questions.trap: Writing just 'qualify the report' - each situation has its own pair: qualified/disclaimer (no evidence) vs qualified/adverse (misstatement or policy).

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: FEMA - External Commercial Borrowings (RBI Master Direction) read with Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (CIRP)
questions.topic: Can a company under CIRP raise ECB on a director's suggestion
questions.ask: Mr. John, also a director of BNC Ltd (under CIRP), suggests BNC should raise ECB for its fund needs. Is it permissible? Give the legal background.
questions.clue: BNC Limited (a company under corporate insolvency resolution process), suggested the ECB route
think: Two laws meet: ECB (FEMA) and CIRP (IBC) - the words 'under corporate insolvency resolution process' are the real test.
Not sure where it sits -> A-Z index: 'ECB - entities under restructuring/CIRP', and 'IBC - management of corporate debtor (s.17), CoC approval (s.28)'.
ECB rule: a company under CIRP can raise ECB only if the resolution plan specifically permits it.
IBC: board suspended, RP runs the company, new finance needs CoC approval -> Mr. John's suggestion alone counts for nothing.

look_up.where: SPOM-A Economic Laws - FEMA (ECB Master Direction); IBC 2016 ss.14, 17, 28

questions.solve: ECB framework: an entity under a restructuring scheme or CIRP can raise ECB only if it is specifically permitted under the resolution plan. Related windows: eligible borrowers taking part in a CIRP as resolution applicants may raise ECB (approval route, not from foreign branches/subsidiaries of Indian banks) to repay the target's rupee term loans; stressed SMA-2/NPA manufacturing and infrastructure borrowers may use ECB under a one-time settlement. IBC: from the CIRP start, the board's powers are suspended and vest in the IRP/RP (s.17); a moratorium applies (s.14); the RP cannot raise interim finance or enter into transactions outside the ordinary course without prior CoC approval (s.28). So BNC's directors, including Mr. John, cannot take this decision.
questions.answer:
Provisions:
1. ECB Master Direction - an entity under CIRP can raise ECB only if specifically permitted under the resolution plan; resolution applicants may raise ECB (approval route) to repay rupee term loans of the target company.
2. IBC - on CIRP, board powers are suspended and management vests in the IRP/RP (s.17); moratorium (s.14); raising finance or acts outside ordinary course need prior CoC approval (s.28).
Analysis: BNC is under CIRP. Mr. John's powers as BNC director are suspended, so his suggestion has no legal force. ECB is not an ordinary-course act.
Conclusion: The suggestion is not permissible as made. BNC can use the ECB route only if the approved resolution plan specifically allows it, and the decision lies with the RP with CoC approval.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI - ICAI printed two answers (ECB only if permitted under the resolution plan; not permissible under IBC); this answer combines both.
questions.flag: ICAI accepted two angles (FEMA-ECB and IBC); write both in 2-3 lines each to be safe.
questions.trap: Answering only ECB eligibility (eligible borrower, all-in-cost, MAMP) and missing that BNC is under CIRP.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: GST - Input Tax Credit (s.16(2) 180-day rule, s.17(5) blocked credits) and interest u/s 50
questions.topic: Responding to GST audit findings: ITC reversal, interest, form of payment
questions.ask: Explain CA Avinash's reply to the five GST audit points, compute ITC to be reversed and interest for non-payment to the supplier within 180 days, and name the form for payment.
questions.clue: reverse the input tax credit claimed being blocked credit
think: 'Within 180 days' -> s.16(2) second proviso + Rule 37; 'blocked credit' -> s.17(5); interest on ITC availed and utilised -> s.50(3) @18%.
Chapter clear -> IDT SM -> Input Tax Credit -> blocked credits list; 'Payment of tax' -> interest.

Item by item: (i) count days, reverse, compute interest; (ii) canteen and (iii) leave travel blocked (not obligatory by law); (iv) 30-seat buses allowed, car insurance/repairs blocked; (v) outdoor catering blocked.
So Avinash accepts (i), (ii), (iii), the car part of (iv) and (v), and contests the buses Rs 12,96,000.

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT - GST Input Tax Credit (ss.16, 17(5)); Payment of Tax (s.50)

questions.solve: (i) Invoice 25.10.2021; 180 days = 6 (Oct) + 30 + 31 + 31 + 28 + 31 + 23 (Apr) -> ends 23.04.2022. ITC Rs 14,04,000 (78,00,000 x 18%) had to be reversed in GSTR-3B for April 2022 (due 20.05.2022) with interest @18% from utilisation. Days 20.11.2021 to 20.05.2022 = 10 + 31 + 31 + 28 + 31 + 30 + 20 = 181; interest = 14,04,000 x 18% x 181/365 = Rs 1,25,321. If never reversed and squared off only in GSTR-3B for August 2022 (filed 18.09.2022), days = 302; interest = 14,04,000 x 18% x 302/365 = Rs 2,09,100. Since the supplier was paid on 20.08.2022, the credit can be re-availed (third proviso to s.16(2)). (ii) Food and beverages for canteen Rs 6,72,000 + 7,50,000 = Rs 14,22,000 - blocked u/s 17(5)(b)(i) unless a law makes it obligatory (e.g. Factories Act canteen for 250+ workers - not stated). (iii) Home travel for employees on leave Rs 6,48,000 - blocked u/s 17(5)(b)(iii). (iv) Buses of 30 seats - block covers only vehicles up to 13 seats -> Rs 12,96,000 allowed; insurance and repairs of cars Rs 96,000 blocked u/s 17(5)(ab). (v) Outdoor catering for customer event Rs 1,26,000 - blocked u/s 17(5)(b)(i). Total = 14,04,000 + 14,22,000 + 6,48,000 + 96,000 + 1,26,000 = Rs 36,96,000.
questions.answer:
Reply of CA Avinash, item-wise:
(i) Agree - supplier not paid within 180 days (ended 23.04.2022): ITC Rs 14,04,000 to be reversed with interest; re-availed after payment on 20.08.2022.
Interest @18% u/s 50(3) = 14,04,000 x 18% x 181/365 = Rs 1,25,321 (reversal in April 2022 GSTR-3B, 20.05.2022). [If not reversed till GSTR-3B of Aug 2022 filed 18.09.2022: x 302/365 = Rs 2,09,100.]
(ii) Agree - canteen food and beverages blocked, s.17(5)(b)(i): Rs 14,22,000.
(iii) Agree - leave/home travel blocked, s.17(5)(b)(iii): Rs 6,48,000.
(iv) Contest buses - 30-seat buses are outside s.17(5)(a): Rs 12,96,000 allowed. Agree on car insurance/repairs, s.17(5)(ab): Rs 96,000.
(v) Agree - outdoor catering blocked, s.17(5)(b)(i): Rs 1,26,000.
Total ITC to be reversed = Rs 36,96,000 (of which Rs 14,04,000 is re-available as the supplier has been paid). Interest @18% also on (ii) to (v) from utilisation to reversal.
Form: no demand has been raised, so reverse ITC and pay interest through GSTR-3B; a voluntary payment of audit dues before SCN may also be intimated in DRC-03.
questions.icai: Same figures as ICAI (Rs 36,96,000; interest Rs 1,25,321 or Rs 2,09,100); ICAI names GSTR-3B as the form.
questions.flag: Form: ICAI says GSTR-3B; dues accepted after a GST audit are commonly paid voluntarily before SCN with intimation in DRC-03 (s.73(5), Rule 142(2)) - mention both.
questions.trap: Reversing the bus ITC too - the 13-seat limit blocks only small vehicles; 30-seat buses are allowed.

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Companies Act, 2013 - Section 188 Related Party Transactions (Rule 15, Meetings of Board Rules)
questions.topic: Holding-WOS sale below market price - Board approval needed, members' approval exempt
questions.ask: SKL (wholly owned subsidiary, accounts consolidated) sold Rs 62 crore of steel to KAL below market price with no approval; SKL's turnover is Rs 610 crore. Was it done correctly?

options.a: No - a special resolution was needed as it exceeds 10% of turnover
options.b: No - an ordinary resolution was needed as it exceeds 10% of turnover
options.c: No - Board consent by a resolution at a meeting was needed
options.d: No approval is needed as it is between holding and WOS with consolidated accounts

questions.clue: wholly owned subsidiaries and whose accounts are consolidated with KAL
think: Sale between holding and subsidiary = related party transaction -> s.188.
Chapter clear -> SPOM-A Companies Act -> s.188, Rule 15(3) thresholds and the provisos.
'Price less than market price' -> not at arm's length -> Board approval at a meeting is a must.
62/610 = 10.2% crosses the 10% limit, but the proviso exempts holding-WOS deals (accounts consolidated and placed before members) from the members' resolution only -> (C).

look_up.where: SPOM-A Corporate Laws - Companies Act s.188, Rule 15

questions.solve: SKL is KAL's WOS, so they are related parties; sale of goods is covered by s.188(1)(a). Selling below market price is not at arm's length, so the ordinary-course exemption fails and consent of the Board by a resolution at a meeting is required. Value Rs 62 crore = 10.16% of Rs 610 crore turnover, which would normally need an ordinary resolution (Rule 15(3): 10% of turnover). But a proviso to s.188(1) exempts transactions between a holding company and its WOS whose accounts are consolidated and placed before shareholders from the members' resolution. So only Board approval was needed - and it was missing. KAL's later ordinary resolution does not cure that.
questions.answer: (C) No - SKL should have entered into the transaction only after Board consent given by a resolution at a meeting.
questions.trap: Picking (B) because 62/610 > 10% - the WOS proviso removes the members' resolution, not the Board's consent.

questions.subject: DT
questions.chapter: Transfer Pricing - Associated Enterprises (s.92A) and comparability data (Rule 10B(4))
questions.topic: Deemed AE through dependence on technology; which year's data the AO can use
questions.ask: KAL's robotic arms depend wholly on Novelty Inc.'s technology; Novelty controls TVIDIA, to whom KAL exported 'UNO'. Do s.92-92F apply, and was the AO right to finally use current-year uncontrolled prices?

options.a: Novelty-KAL are deemed AEs, so TVIDIA is covered too; AO's action at assessment is not valid
options.b: Novelty-KAL are deemed AEs but not KAL-TVIDIA, so not covered; AO's action not valid
options.c: Novelty-KAL are deemed AEs, so TVIDIA is covered too; AO's action at assessment is valid
options.d: Neither pair are AEs; not covered; AO's action not valid

questions.clue: manufacturing of Robotic Arms is wholly dependent on technology provided by Novelty Inc.
think: 'Wholly dependent on technology' -> deemed AE test in s.92A(2) (dependence on know-how/patents of the other).
Chapter clear -> DT SM -> Transfer Pricing -> s.92A(2) list; then Rule 10B(4) on which year's data.
KAL-Novelty deemed AEs; Novelty controls TVIDIA, so the same person participates in both -> KAL and TVIDIA are AEs (s.92A(1)(b)).
Rule 10B(4): use data of the year of the transaction (prior 2 years only as support) -> AO's final action valid -> (C).

look_up.where: ICAI SM DT (International Taxation) - Transfer Pricing

questions.solve: S.92A(2): two enterprises are deemed AEs if goods made by one are wholly dependent on know-how, patents or similar rights owned by the other. KAL's robotic arms depend wholly on Novelty's IK technology -> KAL and Novelty are AEs. Novelty is TVIDIA's holding company and controls its decisions; so the same enterprise (Novelty) participates in the management/control of both KAL and TVIDIA -> KAL and TVIDIA are AEs (s.92A(1)(b)), and export of UNO to TVIDIA is an international transaction. Rule 10B(4): comparability data must be of the financial year in which the transaction took place; data of up to two earlier years can only be used in addition if it affects the price. The AO's first use of only the preceding year was wrong; his later use of current-year data is valid.
questions.answer: (C) Novelty and KAL are deemed AEs, so TVIDIA is also covered by transfer pricing; the AO's action at assessment (current-year data) is valid.
questions.trap: Stopping at KAL-Novelty and missing that common control by Novelty makes TVIDIA an AE too (B).

questions.subject: Costing
questions.chapter: SCMPE (SPOM Set B) - Automation and innovation (SM 5.6, 7.16)

questions.subject: DT
questions.chapter: Transfer Pricing - Most appropriate method (s.92C, Rule 10C)
questions.topic: Meaning of most appropriate method and factors for selecting it
questions.ask: Explain what 'most appropriate method' means and guide GM Accounts on the factors to consider while selecting it for the TVIDIA transactions.
questions.clue: no idea about which is the most appropriate method and how he should select it
think: 'Most appropriate method' is a defined phrase -> s.92C(1) + Rule 10C.
Chapter clear -> DT SM -> Transfer Pricing -> 'most appropriate method' -> Rule 10C(2) factors.
Write the meaning in 2 lines, then the 6 factors; tie 2-3 of them to KAL's export of UNO to TVIDIA.
If you know Rule 10C by heart, write without the book and bank time for 2.7/2.8.

look_up.where: ICAI SM DT (International Taxation) - Transfer Pricing, Rule 10C

questions.solve: S.92C(1): ALP is found by one of the prescribed methods (CUP, RPM, CPM, PSM, TNMM, other method) being the most appropriate method. Rule 10C(1): the most appropriate method is the one best suited to the facts of the transaction and which gives the most reliable measure of ALP. Rule 10C(2) factors: (i) nature and class of the international transaction; (ii) class of AEs and functions performed, considering assets employed and risks assumed; (iii) availability, coverage and reliability of data needed for the method; (iv) degree of comparability between the international and uncontrolled transactions and between the enterprises; (v) extent to which reliable and accurate adjustments can be made for differences; (vi) nature, extent and reliability of assumptions required. Application: for export of UNO, CUP suits if prices of UNO/similar products to unrelated buyers are available; if TVIDIA resells without value addition, RPM; otherwise TNMM.
questions.answer:
Meaning: Under s.92C(1) read with Rule 10C(1), the most appropriate method is the prescribed method best suited to the facts and circumstances of the international transaction, which gives the most reliable measure of the arm's length price.
Factors to consider (Rule 10C(2)):
1. Nature and class of the international transaction (export of product UNO).
2. Class of AEs and functions performed by them, considering assets employed and risks assumed (KAL manufactures; TVIDIA buys/distributes).
3. Availability, coverage and reliability of data needed for the method.
4. Degree of comparability between the international transaction and uncontrolled transactions, and between the enterprises.
5. Extent to which reliable and accurate adjustments can be made for differences.
6. Nature, extent and reliability of assumptions the method needs.
Guidance: if KAL sells UNO or similar products to unrelated buyers, CUP gives the most reliable ALP; if not, RPM (if TVIDIA only resells) or TNMM. Use data of the year of the transaction and record why other methods were rejected (Rule 10D documentation).
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (meaning + the six Rule 10C factors); the application to UNO is added.
questions.trap: Listing the six methods instead of the selection factors that were asked.

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Bond refunding decision (AFM)
questions.topic: When refunding is feasible, NPV method, overlapping interest
questions.ask: As financial advisor, state when the CFO's idea of refunding the 5-year bonds (issued 2 years ago) at a lower rate is feasible, which method decides it, and whether extra interest cost arises.
questions.clue: engage financial advisors to explore refunding options
think: 'Refunding options' + 'lower interest rate' after a rating upgrade -> bond refunding decision (AFM).
Not sure which AFM chapter -> A-Z index: 'refunding', 'call premium'.
Three asks -> three short blocks: conditions (call feature, call premium, rate gap), method (NPV of refunding), extra cost (overlap interest).
Add: discount after-tax savings at after-tax cost of new debt; use case facts - 3 years left, rating improved.

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM - A-Z index 'bond refunding'

questions.solve: Feasible only if (1) the existing bonds carry a call option, so KAL can redeem before maturity; (2) the fall in coupon from the better rating is large enough to cover the call premium (paid over face value), issue costs of new bonds and overlapping interest; (3) new bonds can be raised for the remaining 3 years at the lower rate. Method: NPV of refunding - PV of annual after-tax interest savings over the remaining life, discounted at the after-tax cost of new debt, less net initial outlay (call premium net of tax, new issue costs net of tax shield, overlap interest net of tax, less tax shield on unamortised old issue costs). Refund if NPV > 0. Extra interest: yes - new bonds are usually issued before the old ones are called, so for the overlap period interest is paid on both issues; it is part of the initial outlay.
questions.answer:
1. When feasible:
- Existing bonds must have a call feature (right to redeem before maturity).
- Call premium (amount above face value) is payable - savings must exceed it.
- New bonds at a lower coupon (improved rating) for the remaining 3 years, net of issue costs.
2. Method: Net Present Value of refunding.
- Inflows: PV of annual after-tax interest savings (old coupon - new coupon) over the remaining life, at the after-tax cost of new debt.
- Outflows: call premium, issue costs of new bonds, overlap interest (all net of tax).
- Refund if PV of savings > PV of outflows (NPV positive).
3. Extra interest: Yes. New bonds are generally issued before old bonds are redeemed to avoid a funding gap, so interest runs on both for the overlap period - include it in the initial outlay.
Conclusion: Advise refunding only if the bonds are callable and the NPV of refunding is positive.
questions.trap: Saying refunding is always feasible after a rating upgrade - without a call feature KAL would have to buy back bonds at market price.

questions.chapter: Ind AS 103 Business Combinations with Ind AS 110, Ind AS 38 and Ind AS 116
questions.topic: Controlling stake in a cricket franchise - acquisition method, intangibles, lease, NCI, goodwill
questions.ask: Explain how KAL's Rs 2,500 crore investment for a 70% stake in GSB Warriors is structured, accounted for under Ind AS and how it affects the financial statements.
questions.clue: acquiring a controlling stake (70%) in GSB Warriors
think: 'Controlling stake' in an existing team = acquisition of a business -> Ind AS 103; consolidate under Ind AS 110.
Chapter clear -> FR SM -> Ind AS 103 acquisition method; then Ind AS 38 (franchise rights, player contracts) and Ind AS 116 (leased stadium).
Walk the steps: acquirer and date, consideration (cash + shares at fair value), identifiable assets/liabilities at fair value, goodwill and NCI.
End with Balance Sheet and P&L impact; note the case says 70% and later 60% - either gives control (assume 70%).

look_up.where: ICAI SM FR - Ind AS 103, Ind AS 38, Ind AS 116, Ind AS 110

questions.solve: Structure: KAL buys 70% (the case also says 60% - either gives control) for Rs 2,500 crore paid in cash and KAL shares; 30% stays with old owners -> NCI. Accounting: GSB becomes a subsidiary; Ind AS 103 acquisition method; line-by-line consolidation (Ind AS 110). Consideration = cash + fair value of KAL shares issued on acquisition date; acquisition costs expensed. Identifiable assets at fair value: franchise rights Rs 1,500 crore - intangible; no term given, so indefinite life -> not amortised, tested for impairment every year; player contracts Rs 500 crore - finite-life intangible, amortised over contract terms; working capital/other assets Rs 500 crore at fair value; leased stadium - lease liability at PV of remaining payments and ROU of the same amount, adjusted for favourable/unfavourable terms. Goodwill = consideration + NCI - net identifiable assets; NCI at fair value or proportionate share (choice per deal). Illustration: if Rs 2,500 crore is paid for 70% and net assets (excluding the lease) are Rs 2,500 crore, proportionate NCI = Rs 750 crore and goodwill = 2,500 + 750 - 2,500 = Rs 750 crore; if consideration were lower than net assets, bargain purchase gain to capital reserve.
questions.answer:
1. Structure: KAL acquires a 70% controlling stake for Rs 2,500 crore (cash + equity); 30% stays with old owners (NCI). GSB Warriors becomes a subsidiary.
2. Accounting (Ind AS 103 - acquisition method):
- Consideration: cash + fair value of KAL shares issued; transaction costs to P&L.
- Franchise rights Rs 1,500 crore: intangible; no definite term given -> indefinite life, no amortisation, annual impairment test (Ind AS 36/38).
- Player contracts Rs 500 crore: finite-life intangible, amortised over contract periods.
- Working capital and other assets Rs 500 crore: at fair value.
- Leased stadium and training facility: lease liability (PV of remaining payments) and ROU asset (Ind AS 116).
- Goodwill = consideration + NCI - fair value of net identifiable assets; if negative, bargain purchase gain (capital reserve).
- NCI 30%: at fair value or proportionate share of net assets.
3. Impact on consolidated statements:
- Balance Sheet: franchise rights, player contracts, ROU and goodwill as non-current assets; working capital in current assets; lease liability split current/non-current; NCI in equity; KAL's share capital/premium rises for shares issued.
- P&L: new revenue (broadcasting, sponsorship, tickets, merchandise); amortisation of player contracts, depreciation of ROU, interest on lease liability, impairment if any; profit split between owners and NCI.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI; ICAI's line that consideration 'forms part of equity share capital' is read here as: only KAL shares issued as consideration raise KAL's share capital.
questions.flag: Case says 70% and later 60% - ICAI used 70% (NCI 30%); ICAI's equity line is loosely worded - consideration paid is not GSB's share capital on consolidation.
questions.trap: Amortising franchise rights without a stated term - with no definite term treat it as indefinite life: impairment test only.

questions.topic: Five forces applied to MBL's solar bike launch
questions.ask: Summarise the issues MBL must tackle under Porter's Five Forces for its solar bike launch - with reference to the case facts, not abstract theory.

Note the warning 'not a mere abstract reference' - every force must carry a case fact.

Map facts: Rs 100 crore R&D and patents (new entrants); petrol bikes and 20 EV makers (substitutes); only 3 weak solar rivals (rivalry); solar panels/batteries (suppliers); distributors and price-sensitive buyers (buyers).
End with 'key issues' + 3-4 actions - that is what 'summary of issues to be tackled' asks for.

look_up.where: ICAI SM SPOM Set B (SCMPE) - Ch 1, Porter's Five Forces (1.34)

questions.solve: New entrants - low: Rs 100 crore R&D before regular operations, unique patented technology, MBL's existing market presence and logistics; but 20 EV makers could add solar later. Substitutes - moderate: petrol two-wheelers and plain EVs; rising fuel prices and OPEC dependence push buyers towards solar. Rivalry - low now: only 3 solar players without superior technology or visibility; may rise as bigger EV players enter. Suppliers - low to moderate: spares are patented and sold only through MBL's distributors; but solar panels and batteries may come from a few, often imported, suppliers. Buyers - moderate: distributors are tied to MBL; end customers may resist a price with 50% mark-up and compare with cheaper EVs. Issues: keep the technology lead, secure critical inputs, justify the premium price, prepare for new entrants. Actions: patents + continuous R&D; long-term contracts or backward integration for panels/batteries; awareness of fuel savings; cheaper variants later.
questions.answer:
Porter's Five Forces - MBL's solar bike 'Powerhouse':
1. Threat of new entrants - Low: Rs 100 crore R&D needed before operations, patented technology, MBL's existing brand and logistics. Issue: 20 EV makers can move into solar - keep innovating.
2. Threat of substitutes - Moderate: petrol two-wheelers and EVs without solar. Rising fuel prices and OPEC dependence favour solar. Issue: show running-cost savings.
3. Rivalry - Low for now: only 3 solar makers, none with superior technology or visibility. Issue: rivalry will rise as large EV/global players enter.
4. Bargaining power of suppliers - Low to moderate: patented spares controlled by MBL; but solar panels and batteries depend on a few (often imported) suppliers. Issue: input supply and price risk.
5. Bargaining power of buyers - Moderate: distributors bound to MBL's channel; end buyers price-sensitive vs a 50% mark-up. Issue: premium price may slow adoption.
Actions: protect patents and keep R&D going; long-term contracts/backward integration for panels and batteries; customer awareness on savings and green benefits; launch lower-priced variants later to widen the market.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (ICAI notes alternative views are possible).
questions.trap: Writing the textbook model with no case facts - the question says such an answer will not score.
